newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany shudders as mark branded weak by markets.
newsitem.headline: Germany shudders as mark branded weak by markets.

text.p: Germany on Tuesday signalled growing concern that the country could be on the brink of losing one of its most cherished assets -- the unquestioning faith in the strength of its currency, the mark.

In the second leg of a two-pronged offensive against the strengthening dollar, Finance Minister Theo Waigel added his weight to comments from Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer last week, making clear a recent fall in the mark was overdone.

"We are interested in a strong deutschemark. I think what's happening at the moment is an overreaction of the markets," Waigel told a news conference in Berlin in response to a question about the strength of the dollar and sterling.

"We have, as in the past, agreed cooperation within the G7," Waigel added, making a veiled threat that the Group of Seven industrial nations could enter markets with joint action to support the mark. "We are in contact with our partners."

Tietmeyer, speaking last week with the dollar at a rate against the mark of about 1.76 marks -- well below the current level of about 1.7950 -- said the phase of correction in the dollar from 1995's record lows had "clearly come to an end".
Sterling similarly stuck near to 6-1/2 year highs, trading just above 3.02 marks.

Analysts said the dismissive market response was a bitter reflection of the marked loss of standing Germany has suffered in recent months -- as it battles against itself to qualify for European monetary union -- and saw no mark recovery in sight.

"The statement from...Waigel that the strength in the pound and dollar is an overreaction from markets, shows the ignorance or perhaps helplessness of the administration of (Chancellor Helmut) Kohl with respect to the mark weakness, which has been triggered by the verbal loosening of the Maastricht criteria," analysts at ABN Amro said in a commentary.
"That means the mark weakness will continue," they added.
The mark's weakness comes at a critical point for Germany, with the planned launch of the European single currency now less than 18 months away.

Tietmeyer in his comments made the point that it was essential that the mark go into the joint currency from a position of strength. Strategic use of a weak currency to promote trade is anathema to inflation-conscious Germans.

But in a vicious circle of economic argument, wrangling over the precise fiscal criteria for monetary union -- and the various accounting methods one could adopt to reach them -- has damaged the credibility of the euro, and of the mark.
Goldman Sachs chief economist Thomas Mayer said it was clear that the present currency problems were no longer a question of a strong dollar or sterling, but of a weak mark.
"The exchange rate developments are disturbing. They demonstrate a certain mistrust in the government's EMU policy."

At issue is Bonn's absolute insistence that the entry criterion on fiscal deficits, which states that budget deficits must not exceed three percent of gross domestic product, be interpreted to mean 3.0 percent is the ceiling.

With Germany itself on course to miss the target unless it implements the strictest spending cuts, Bonn's attempts to raise cash by seemingly any means have hurt Germany's image as the voice of reason in international debates.

Even the ultra-conservative Bundesbank has steered clear of tying itself down to the 3.0 percent definition. Wary of problems in meeting the goal, it stresses sustainability as its main litmus test for countries' EMU entry.

In this environment, with German verbal support for the currency seemingly ineffective, analysts gave credence to market talk that the central bank could free up its securities repurchase rate, allowing it to drift gradually higher.

The Bundesbank has kept a tight rein on the repo rate for over a year now, setting its regular securities repurchase tenders at a fixed interest rate of three percent rather than allowing banks to bid at different interest rates for funds.
"German monetary policy is quite expansive at the moment... and the government and central bank cannot remain indifferent if the mark slides still further," Mayer said.
